newsitem.title: USA: MFN denial for China would hurt U.S. -- GM.
newsitem.headline: MFN denial for China would hurt U.S. -- GM.

text.p: If the U.S. Congress rejects renewal of China's trade privileges, U.S. companies would lose economic opportunities in China that would simply go to other countries, General Motors Corp Chairman Jack Smith said Thursday.

Smith, speaking to reporters at a briefing, said renewal of China's most-favored-nation trade status was important for the future of U.S. business ventures in China, such as GM's new mid-size car plant in Shanghai.
Denial of MFN would "cut off the U.S. economic opportunity with China," he said.
"I don't think that's wise," he added.

"What is the United States going to gain? It's going to gain nothing." Smith said. "China can do business with any country in the world and will do business and has shown that. Any time we have specific sanctions, they go to France and buy whatever they want, or go somewhere else."
Holding up MFN over human rights would help to destroy the U.S. commercial base in China, he said.

GM is building a mid-size car plant with Shanghai Automotive Industry Corp that is eventually expected to produce 100,000 Buick sedans annually. GM also is trying to negotiate a deal to take over a small car plant in Guangzhou that PSA Peugeot Citroen plans to pull out of.
Smith said the GM proposal calls for production of a small Opel model at the plant, possibly the Astra, and construction of a new engine plant in the southern Chinese city.
"There's no guarantee that we're going to win that, but we're in a pretty good position to negotiate," he said of the Guangzhou venture.
He said part of Peugeot's problem in Guangzhou stemmed from the fact that the car produced there was an older model. GM hopes to install much newer technology, Smith said.
